blocks.heading: Retained profit and spendable cash
blocks.text: Retained profit is profit kept within the business instead of distributed to owners. It forms part of accumulated equity, not a promise that an equal cash balance exists. The retained value may be employed in machinery, inventory or receivables. Spendable cash depends on actual cash and bank balances, payment commitments and any reserve needed for operations. A business can retain a profit and still need to collect debtors before buying equipment. Selling a surplus asset may release cash without creating the same amount of profit. Internal financing decisions should therefore test whether funds are genuinely available rather than quoting retained profit alone. A large accumulated balance of retained earnings can coexist with limited liquidity.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eno Print retains N$30,000 profit for the year but spends N$25,000 cash on a machine. For this illustration assume all retained profit was initially received in cash and there are no other movements or opening cash. After the purchase, cash remaining from those funds is N$5,000. The retained profit is still N$30,000 under the simplified assumptions, but much of the value is now held in equipment. It cannot pay N$30,000 to a supplier merely by pointing to retained profit.
